steps.text: You just chose one prize over another, and you probably took the rook. [I] Players seem to have turned that feeling into numbers called **counting values**: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king has no number because it is never taken; it is checkmated. Next comes the table on a board, then a worked capture before any question.

steps.caption: The counting values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The knight and bishop share a number.

claims.statement: A white pawn stands on f2.
A white knight stands on e1.
A white bishop stands on d1.
A white rook stands on c1.
A white queen stands on b1.

steps.caption: A worked example first. White's knight can take an undefended rook. Nothing can take the knight back.

line.say: The knight takes the rook. Nothing guards it, so White wins 5 points and loses nothing.

claims.statement: The knight wins the rook and nothing comes back.
No black piece guards the rook.

steps.caption: Colour makes no difference. Here it is Black's turn, and Black's knight can take a white rook.

line.say: The black knight takes the white rook: Black wins 5 points. The value belongs to the piece, not to its colour.

claims.statement: The black knight wins the rook for nothing.
No white piece guards the rook.
